english: I came to buy a SIM card
usage: I came to buy a SIM card
Polite; said as you walk into a phone shop or convenience store
I'm here to get a SIM
반말, only with a friend tagging along, not to staff
Straight request once you know they have it
선불 ('prepaid') vs. 후불 ('postpaid') — ask which they sell
examples: 유심 사러 왔어요.
I came to buy a SIM card.
Opening line as you reach the counter; 사러 왔다 = 'came in order to buy'
외국인인데 유심 사러 왔어요. 여권 보여 드릴까요?
I'm a foreigner, I came for a SIM — should I show my passport?
유심 registration needs ID; offer your 여권 ('passport') up front
여행용으로 쓸 건데 선불 유심 사러 왔어요.
I came for a prepaid SIM to use while traveling.
선불 ('prepaid') signals you don't want a contract
nuance: 유심 is the Korean pronunciation of 'USIM' (the chip), and it's the everyday word — Koreans almost never say 'SIM card' in English; they say 유심. The pattern 사러 왔어요 is verb-stem + -(으)러 ('in order to') + 왔어요 ('came'), literally 'I came in order to buy', which is exactly how you state your purpose on entering a shop. Default to 존댓말 with staff; the 반말 유심 사러 왔어 is only for a friend. A key contrast: 사러 왔어요 announces WHY you're here, while 유심 하나 주세요 ('one SIM, please') is the direct order — open with the first, then move to the second once they confirm stock. The big English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 유심 카드 살 수 있어요? ('can I buy a SIM card?'), which is understandable but sounds like you're checking your own ability or permission; the natural opener is the purpose statement 사러 왔어요. Also don't attach the object particle and say 유심을 사러 — in speech the 을 is usually dropped. Note 유심 (the chip) is different from 개통 (activating service); buying the chip and activating the line are two steps.

english: I came to activate my phone
usage: Polite; the standard opener at a carrier shop
I'm here to set up my phone
반말, only with a friend, never to staff
Could you activate it for me?
Direct request once you're at the desk
I'm looking to activate a new line
examples: 개통하러 왔어요.
I came to activate a phone.
Said at the counter of an SKT/KT/LG U+ shop
유심 샀는데 개통하러 왔어요.
I bought a SIM and came to activate it.
Sequence it: you have the 유심, now you want 개통
외국인 등록증으로 개통할 수 있어요? 개통하러 왔어요.
Can I activate with my ARC? I came to set up service.
외국인 등록증 (ARC) is the ID foreigners use to 개통
nuance: 개통 (Sino-Korean 開通, 'opening through') means activating a phone line so it can actually make calls and use data — the moment your number goes live. The pattern is again -(으)러 왔어요 ('came in order to'), so 개통하러 왔어요 = 'I came to activate.' Say this in 존댓말 to staff. The crucial contrast is 개통 vs. 가입: 가입 ('signing up/joining', 加入) is enrolling in a carrier/plan as a subscriber, while 개통 is the technical act of turning the line on — when you start fresh you often do both, but if you ask only for 개통 with no plan chosen, staff will ask about 요금제 (the plan) and 약정 (contract) first. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 폰 켜러 왔어요 ('I came to turn the phone ON'), but 켜다 means powering the device on, not activating service — use 개통. Another is over-translating 'set up' as 셋업/설정, which sounds like configuring settings, not registering a line. Keep 개통 for the line going live. Foreigners should be ready with 외국인 등록증 (ARC) or 여권 since 개통 legally requires ID.

켜다 is to power the device ON (the screen). Activating the line/number is 개통: say 개통하러 왔어요.
Using 셋업하러 / 설정하러 왔어요.
셋업/설정 sound like configuring phone settings, not registering a line. The right word for going live is 개통.
Confusing 개통 with 가입.
가입 is becoming a subscriber (joining a plan/carrier); 개통 is the line being switched on. Mention 요금제 if you also need to pick a plan, since 개통 alone doesn't choose one.

usage: Polite; hand the choice to the staff
반말, to a friend who knows carriers
Asking specifically for the budget option
Is there a plan that fits me?
Asking them to match a plan to your usage
examples: 요금제 추천해 주세요.
Could you recommend a plan?
Said when you can't decide among the options
데이터 많이 쓰는데, 요금제 추천해 주세요.
I use a lot of data — could you recommend a plan?
State your usage (데이터 많이 쓰다) so the pick fits
통화는 거의 안 하고 데이터만 써요. 요금제 추천해 주세요.
I barely call, I only use data — please recommend a plan.
Contrast 통화 (calls) vs. 데이터 to guide their suggestion
nuance: 요금제 (요금 'fee/charge' + 제 'system', 料金制) is the monthly PLAN — the bundle of data, calls, and texts at a set price. 추천해 주세요 is 추천하다 ('recommend', 推薦) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'), the favor form that politely asks staff to choose for you. Default 존댓말. A precise contrast: 요금제 is the recurring plan, while 약정 is the CONTRACT term (how long you're locked in) and 기기값/단말기 is the phone's price — newcomers blur these, but staff treat them as three separate questions. Another near-synonym issue: don't say 플랜 추천해 주세요 using the English 'plan' — Koreans say 요금제; 플랜 sounds off in this context. The English-speaker pitfall is the favor-verb trap: saying bare 요금제 추천하세요 is an imperative ('you, recommend!') that sounds bossy, and 요금제 추천 주세요 is ungrammatical because you can't 'give' a recommendation — it must be 추천 + 해 + 주세요. To get a concrete answer, pair it with your usage: 데이터 많이 써요 ('I use lots of data') or 통화 많이 해요 ('I call a lot') so they can match 요금제 to you.

The English 'plan' (플랜) is unnatural here. The word for a phone plan is 요금제: 요금제 추천해 주세요.
Saying 요금제 추천하세요 to staff.
Bare 추천하세요 is a command ('recommend!') and sounds bossy. Use the favor form 추천해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.

usage: Set me up with unlimited data
반말, to a friend helping you pick
I'll go with the unlimited plan
Announcing your own choice at the counter
Checking first whether they offer it
examples: 데이터 무제한으로 해 주세요.
Please make it unlimited data.
Said when picking your 요금제 so you never run out
유튜브 많이 봐서 데이터 무제한으로 해 주세요.
I watch a lot of YouTube, so make it unlimited data.
Give the reason (유튜브 많이 보다) for going unlimited
완전 무제한이에요, 아니면 속도 제한 있어요?
Is it truly unlimited, or is there a speed limit?
Many 'unlimited' plans throttle (속도 제한) after a cap — ask
nuance: 데이터 (loanword 'data') 무제한 (無制限, 'no limit') is the unlimited-data option, and 무제한으로 해 주세요 uses -(으)로 ('as/into') + 해 주세요 ('please make it') — 'please set it up AS unlimited.' That -(으)로 marks the result/choice you want, which is the natural particle for selecting an option. Default 존댓말. A real-world contrast every newcomer needs: 완전 무제한 ('fully unlimited', no throttling) vs. plans that are 무제한 only up to a daily cap and then 속도 제한 (speed-throttled) — so 무제한 alone doesn't guarantee full speed; ask 완전 무제한이에요? The particle pitfall for English speakers is the 직역 trap of saying 데이터 무제한을 해 주세요 with the object particle 을 — here you're choosing a setting, so it must be 무제한으로 (with -(으)로), not 무제한을. Another error is treating 무제한 as a verb (무제한해 주세요), but it's a noun/state: you say 무제한으로 해 주세요. Don't confuse 무제한 ('unlimited') with 추가 ('extra/add-on'); if you only want a top-up of data, that's 데이터 추가, a different request.

english: Can I use it without a contract?
usage: Can I use it without a contract?
Polite; asking to avoid being locked in
반말, to a friend who's done it before
무약정 = the no-contract option, stated as your wish
How many months is the contract?
Asking the term length if a contract is required
examples: 약정 없이 쓸 수 있어요?
Can I use it without a contract?
Asked when you don't want a long commitment
한국에 오래 안 있어서 약정 없이 쓸 수 있어요?
I'm not in Korea long — can I use it without a contract?
오래 안 있다 ('not staying long') is the classic reason
약정 없이 쓰면 요금이 더 비싸요?
If I go without a contract, is the fee higher?
약정 often subsidizes the price; ask if 무약정 costs more
nuance: 약정 (約定, 'agreement/commitment') is the CONTRACT term — the period (often 24개월) you promise to stay, usually in exchange for a phone discount. 약정 없이 ('without a contract') + 쓸 수 있어요? ('can I use it?') asks to go commitment-free. Default 존댓말. The exact word for the no-contract option is 무약정 (無約定), so 무약정으로 하고 싶어요 ('I want to go contract-free') is the cleanest way to request it. A critical contrast newcomers miss: 약정 (the commitment period) is NOT the same as 요금제 (the monthly plan) — you can change plans, but breaking an 약정 early triggers a 위약금 (early-termination penalty). The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 계약 없이 — 계약 ('contract') is the general legal word and sounds odd for a phone plan; the industry term is 약정 / 무약정. Another is asking 약정 안 해도 돼요? ('do I not have to commit?'), which works but the crisper phrasing is 약정 없이 쓸 수 있어요? or 무약정 돼요? Be aware: going 무약정 often means no device discount, so the phone may cost more upfront — that's why people ask 약정 없이 쓰면 더 비싸요?

usage: Polite; asking the data allowance of a plan
반말, to a friend comparing plans
기가 ('giga/GB') — the most concrete way to ask
What happens when I use it all up?
Asking about overage / throttling after the cap
examples: 이 요금제 데이터 얼마예요?
How much data does this plan have?
Point at a plan and ask its allowance
데이터 몇 기가예요? 영상 많이 봐요.
How many gigs is it? I watch a lot of video.
기가 is clearer than 얼마; give your usage too
데이터 다 쓰면 속도 느려져요, 아니면 추가 요금이에요?
When I run out, does it slow down, or is there an extra charge?
속도 느려지다 (throttle) vs. 추가 요금 (overage fee)
nuance: 데이터 얼마예요? is 데이터 + 얼마 ('how much') + 예요, asking the size of a plan's data allowance. Note 얼마 normally asks PRICE, so here it's slightly ambiguous; the sharper, unambiguous version is 데이터 몇 기가예요? ('how many gigabytes?') using 기가 (GB), which staff immediately understand as the data amount. Default 존댓말. The contrast to nail: 데이터 몇 기가예요? asks the AMOUNT of data, while 얼마예요? on its own (no 데이터) asks the PRICE of the plan — say the full 데이터 얼마예요? or use 기가 to avoid being misheard as asking the cost. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 데이터 얼마나 많아요? ('how plentiful is the data?'), which sounds like commenting on quantity rather than asking the spec — Koreans ask 몇 기가예요?. Counting GB uses Sino-Korean numbers with 기가: 십 기가 (10GB), not 열 기가.

english: How do I verify my identity?
usage: How do I verify my identity?
Polite; asking how to pass identity verification
How do I do the ID check?
반말, asking a friend walking you through it
The identity verification won't go through
Can foreigners do identity verification too?
Asking if the system accepts non-Koreans
examples: 본인 인증 어떻게 해요?
How do I verify my identity?
When an app/site demands ID verification to proceed
휴대폰 본인 인증이 자꾸 안 돼요. 외국인인데 어떻게 해요?

사인업 isn't Korean. Use 가입 (enroll/join): 가입할 때 뭐 필요해요?
Confusing 가입 with 개통.
가입 is becoming a subscriber (the paperwork); 개통 is the line being switched on. Asking what's needed to 가입 is about ID and documents.
Using object 을 with 필요하다: 서류를 필요해요.
필요하다 ('to be needed') is an adjective; its subject takes 이/가, not 을. Correct: 서류가 필요해요 / 뭐가 필요해요?
